text: This closes chapter four by bringing purging, CPCV, and the deflated Sharpe ratio together into one practical question: how do you tell, before you risk real money, that a backtest is overfit rather than genuinely predictive? The probability of backtest overfitting, from Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, and Zhu, is one direct way to measure exactly that.

PBO works through a CPCV-like construction called combinatorially symmetric cross-validation. You split a strategy's performance history into subsamples and form every possible way to combine half into an in-sample set and the other half into an out-of-sample set. For each combination, you pick whichever configuration looked best in-sample and check whether it ranks above or below the median out-of-sample. PBO is the fraction of combinations where that in-sample winner turns out to be a below-median performer out-of-sample. A high PBO means your selection process is picking up overfitting noise, not skill.

Beyond the formal measure, watch for practical red flags. Backtest decay — a strong backtested Sharpe ratio that quietly erodes once the strategy meets live data — is close to the single most reliable symptom of overfitting. So is a dozen tunable parameters tested against only a few years of data, or a process where every piece of data has already influenced some decision, leaving nothing left to surprise you. The fixes: hold out data untouched until the very end, prefer fewer parameters, write down the hypothesis before testing it, and run CPCV and DSR before trusting the headline number.

The minimum backtest length heuristic ties back to the deflated Sharpe ratio from last lesson. The more configurations you test, the longer your backtest history needs to be before a high in-sample Sharpe ratio means anything, because the expected maximum Sharpe ratio across many trials keeps climbing with trial count. Five configurations over a few years of data is plausible to trust; five thousand over that same stretch is not.

Across this whole chapter, the thread has been the same: a backtest result is only as trustworthy as the discipline used to produce it — time order, purging and embargoing, many combinatorial paths instead of one, and a Sharpe ratio checked against how many things you actually tried. Next, lesson nineteen opens chapter five, feature importance and interpretation, starting with feature importance in financial models.
